title: Employment Tests and Selection Procedures
pub: United States Equal Employment Opportunity Commission
author: United States Equal Employment Opportunity Commission

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source addresses Title VII standards for discriminatory employment tests and selection procedures, not legal AI capability, verification, workflow redesign, or labour-market effects. It therefore provides insufficient evidence to determine a position on the cluster’s proposition.

mo.t: Employment screening: Audits reveal bias without remedying it
Hiring audits: Disclosure cannot guarantee nondiscrimination
Reliable delivery: Legal engineering bridges capability and service

kp.k: Guidance explains employment discrimination requirements, not AI-specific changes
kp.d: Issued December 1, 2007, this EEOC technical assistance document addresses employment testing and selection under federal anti-discrimination laws rather than AI or changes in legal services. It expressly distinguishes its explanatory status from binding law.
qs: This document provides information on employer use of employment tests and selection procedures, and the circumstances under which issues may arise under Title VII, the ADA, or ADEA.
The contents of this document do not have the force and effect of law and are not meant to bind the public in any way.

kp.k: Online applications and security concerns encouraged employment testing
kp.d: The EEOC attributes increased testing partly to post-9-11 security concerns, workplace violence, safety and liability, and employers' desire to screen large online applicant pools efficiently and non-subjectively. It reports that discrimination charges involving testing and exclusions through background checks, credit reports and other selection procedures reached a high point of 304 in FY 2007.
qs: There has been an increase in employment testing due in part to post   9-11 security concerns as well as concerns about workplace violence,   safety, and liability.
the large-scale adoption of online   job applications has motivated employers to seek efficient ways to   screen large numbers of online applicants in a non-subjective way.
reached a high point in FY   2007 at 304 charges.

kp.k: Selection tools can discriminate through intent or exclusionary effects
kp.d: The document recognises testing as potentially effective for identifying qualified applicants and employees, while explaining that intentional discrimination and disproportionate exclusion without legally sufficient justification can violate federal law. Its scope extends beyond formal tests to background and credit checks, performance appraisals and other selection procedures, many administered online.
qs: The use of tests and other selection procedures can be a very effective means of determining which applicants or employees are most qualified for a particular job.

Use of tests and other selection procedures can also violate the federal anti-discrimination laws if they disproportionately exclude people in a particular group by race, sex, or another covered basis, unless the employer can justify the test or procedure under the law.

kp.k: Title VII restricts differential testing and protected-category scoring
kp.d: The EEOC explains that Title VII prohibits intentional selection discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex or national origin. Testing African American applicants' reading ability while not testing white counterparts illustrates disparate treatment. The document separately states that employers cannot adjust scores, cutoffs or results on these protected grounds.
qs: Employers are not permitted to (1) adjust the     scores of, (2) use different cutoff scores for, or (3) otherwise     alter the results of employment-related tests on the basis of race,     color, religion, sex, or national origin.

kp.k: Disparate impact analysis requires job-specific justification and alternatives
kp.d: Under the document's account of Title VII, disparate impact ordinarily requires statistical analysis. Where a procedure disproportionately excludes a protected group, the employer must demonstrate job-relatedness and business necessity tied to safe and efficient performance of the particular job, not merely general skills. Even with that showing, a challenger may identify an equally effective, less discriminatory alternative.
qs: Determining whether a test         or other selection procedure has a disparate impact on a         particular group ordinarily requires a statistical analysis.
An employer can meet this standard by         showing that it is necessary to the safe and efficient         performance of the job.
is another test available that would be equally         effective in predicting job performance but would not         disproportionately exclude the protected group?

kp.k: Employers retain responsibility for validation despite vendor documentation
kp.d: The EEOC describes the 1978 Uniform Guidelines on Employee Selection Procedures as providing three methods of demonstrating job-relatedness through test validation. Its best practices recommend validation for the specific positions and purposes involved, adoption of equally effective alternatives with less adverse impact, and updates as job requirements change. Vendor documentation does not displace employer responsibility.
qs: These methods of demonstrating       job-relatedness are called “test validation.”
While a test vendor’s documentation supporting the validity of a test   may be helpful, the employer is still responsible for ensuring that   its tests are valid under UGESP.

To ensure that a test or selection procedure remains predictive of   success in a job, employers should keep abreast of changes in job   requirements and should update the test specifications or selection   procedures accordingly.

kp.k: ADA medical inquiry restrictions depend on employment stage
kp.d: The document explains that disability-related questions and medical examinations are prohibited before a conditional job offer. After an offer but before work starts, they are permitted if applied to all entering the same job category. For existing employees, they must be job-related and consistent with business necessity; examples include objective evidence supporting concerns about essential functions or direct threats, and accommodation requests where disability or need is not obvious.
qs: The ADA specifies when an employer may require an applicant or     employee to undergo a medical examination, *i.e.*, a procedure or     test that seeks information about an individual’s physical or mental     impairments or health.
The ADA also specifies when an employer may     make “disability-related inquiries,” *i.e.*, inquiries that are     likely to elicit information about a disability.

kp.k: ADA testing must measure skills and accommodate disabilities
kp.d: The EEOC states that tests screening out individuals with disabilities must be justified as job-related and consistent with business necessity. Administration should measure the intended skills or aptitudes rather than impairments, and reasonable accommodations are required for known limitations of otherwise qualified applicants or employees unless they impose undue hardship.
qs: Use employment tests that screen out or tend to screen out an       individual with a disability or a class of individuals with       disabilities unless the test, as used by the employer, is shown to       be job-related and consistent with business necessity.

Fail to make reasonable accommodations, including in the       administration of tests, to the known physical or mental       limitations of an otherwise qualified individual with a disability       who is an applicant or employee, unless such accommodation would       impose an undue hardship.

kp.k: ADEA disparate impact has a distinct reasonableness defence
kp.d: The document describes ADEA protection for people aged 40 and over in hiring, promotion and reductions in force, including prohibitions on intentional age discrimination. Unlike its Title VII account, its ADEA disparate impact discussion specifies a reasonable factor other than age defence, citing Smith v. City of Jackson (2005), and says the employer must show that the selected test or device was reasonable.
qs: The ADEA prohibits discrimination based on age (40 and over) with     respect to any term, condition, or privilege of employment.
Thus, if a test or other     selection procedure has a disparate impact based on age, the     employer must show that the test or device chosen was a reasonable     one.

kp.k: Ford settlement illustrates limits of previously validated tests
kp.d: The EEOC reports that Ford's Apprenticeship Training Selection System measured verbal, numerical and spatial reasoning to evaluate mechanical aptitude. Although validated in 1991, it continued disproportionately to exclude African American applicants; subsequently developed, less discriminatory procedures could have met Ford's needs but were not adopted. A court-approved settlement required replacement with a procedure designed by a jointly selected industrial psychologist and provided $8.55 million in monetary relief. This is reported as a settlement, not an adjudicated finding.
qs: Although it had been validated in 1991, the ATSS   continued to have a statistically significant disparate impact by   excluding African American applicants.
Less discriminatory selection   procedures were subsequently developed that would have served Ford’s   needs, but Ford did not modify its procedures.

kp.k: Dial ruling rejects excessive strength testing and injury justification
kp.d: In EEOC v. Dial Corp., women's share of hires fell from 46% before a strength test to 15% afterward. Dial argued that the test resembled the job and reduced injuries. The EEOC reports expert evidence that the test was considerably harder than the job and injury reductions began two years before implementation, most likely because of improved training and job rotation. The Eighth Circuit upheld the finding of Title VII disparate impact discrimination.
qs: prior to the use of the test, 46% of hires were women;   after use of the test, only 15% of hires were women.

The EEOC established through expert testimony, however, that the test was considerably more   difficult than the job and that the reduction in injuries occurred two   years before the test was implemented, most likely due to improved   training and better job rotation procedures.

kp.k: Daimler Chrysler settlement provides accessible testing and monetary relief
kp.d: The EEOC describes a settlement involving applicants with learning disabilities taking a pre-employment test for hourly unskilled manufacturing jobs. It provided monetary relief for 12 identified individuals and an opportunity to retake the hiring test with a reader. The employer also agreed to provide readers or equivalent audiotapes for applicants requesting a reader and documenting an ADA disability.
qs: The resulting   settlement agreement provided monetary relief for 12 identified   individuals and the opportunity to take the hiring test with the   assistance of a reader.
The accommodation   consisted of either a reader for all instructions and all written parts of the test, or an audiotape providing the same information.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The EEOC makes no AI-specific claims or predictions. In its own domain, it states that employment selection tools can effectively identify qualified candidates but can also violate federal anti-discrimination law.
pts.d: The document concerns employment testing and screening, not AI or changes to legal services. The EEOC states that intentional discrimination and unjustified disproportionate exclusion can make selection procedures unlawful. It also attributes increased testing partly to security, safety and liability concerns, and says online applications have encouraged employers to seek efficient screening methods. These are contemporary observations and legal guidance, not predictions about AI.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The EEOC supports its guidance with statutes, regulations, judicial decisions, enforcement examples and a charge count; it supplies no AI evidence.
pts.d: Legal authorities include Title VII, the ADA, the ADEA and the Uniform Guidelines on Employee Selection Procedures. The document reports 304 relevant discrimination charges in FY 2007. Its examples distinguish settlements from adjudicated findings: Ford settled claims concerning a cognitive test and less discriminatory alternatives; Dial's strength test was found unlawful under Title VII, with the finding upheld on appeal; Daimler Chrysler settled a test-accommodation case. These illustrate employment-selection risks rather than measured AI performance or effects.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Issued December 1, 2007, the document explains existing requirements and ongoing compliance conditions rather than forecasting future developments.
pts.d: The EEOC expressly identifies the document as nonbinding technical assistance. It distinguishes Title VII's job-relatedness and business-necessity standard and consideration of less discriminatory alternatives from the ADEA's reasonable-factor-other-than-age standard. ADA requirements include restrictions on medical examinations and disability-related inquiries, accurate measurement of relevant abilities, and reasonable accommodations subject to undue hardship. Employers are advised to maintain validation as job requirements change; vendor documentation does not transfer responsibility away from the employer.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The affected groups are employers, applicants and employees, particularly people exposed to discriminatory exclusion or inaccessible testing.
pts.d: Employers and HR practitioners must attend to selection procedures' validity, administration, limitations and discriminatory effects. Applicants and employees can face exclusion from hiring or promotion; the ADEA discussion also addresses reductions in force. Protected groups include those defined by race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability and age 40 or older. The examples concern African American apprenticeship applicants, women applying for production jobs, and applicants with learning disabilities needing reading accommodations. No distinct effect on lawyers, law firms or legal-services buyers is asserted.
